About

Who built this, and why.

I am Paula Silva, Developer Solutions Advisor and Software Latam Leader on the Data & AI team, Global Black Belt for Microsoft Americas. My work spans the full AI transformation journey, from application and legacy modernization to agentic architecture and platform engineering, helping enterprise teams adopt AI-assisted development at scale. A deck is a system too: this one is the catalog of how mine are built.

This deck is the master reference of the ms-presentation-deck skill, version 3.0.0: one slide per pattern, nine parts, one hundred and nine slides. Text families, tables, charts, every engineering diagram, reference architectures with the official icons, animated scenes, light-theme product simulations, interactives, media and code. Every slide is generated by the scripts shipped with the skill, so a new deck can copy the rule, not the pixels.

Read it once end to end, then keep it open next to the deck you are building: the speaker notes on every slide say what the pattern is for, when to use it and what to say out loud. Three rules hold everything together: pick the shape, fill the canvas, one hero per part.

Read before

How to use this catalog in a new deck.

Pick the shape

One component per slide

Ask what shape the content has before writing: dates become a timeline, fact plus consequence a ledger, layers a stack, symptom plus fix a red-over-green pair. Three slides in a row on the same component means two are wrong.

Fill the canvas

fillCanvas() does the rest

Every content slide grows type, padding and gaps until it touches the stage; a short slide is a design error, not a font-size problem. Diagrams are drawn on a tall canvas so no label is compressed.

One hero per part

Scene, simulation or interactive

Every part opens with a divider (bars, title, subtitle) and a hero slide that moves: an animated scene, a typed terminal, a light-theme product mock or an interactive that reveals from the first click.

Why it mattersthe audience reads shape before words
The impacta 60-slide deck with 25 archetypes never feels monotonous
The trapcopying the hooks deck instead of copying its rules

function binarySearch(a, x) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
  while (lo <= hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (a[mid] === x) return mid;
    a[mid] < x ? lo = mid + 1 : hi = mid - 1;
  }
  return -1;
}

Ledger

Numbered rows with an icon: fact, then consequence.

01
Timeouts fail open
Every hook, every event, even policy hooks. The process is killed after timeoutSec and the tool proceeds through the normal permission flow.
02
preToolUse is fail-closed
A crashed guard denies the tool. A timeout does not. Keep the script local and under a second.
03
Exit 2 means deny on the gates
On preToolUse and permissionRequest stderr is shown and stdout is ignored, even if it says allow.
04
Output is capped
10 MiB of stdout, 10 KB of additionalContext. Two decision objects make invalid JSON and are dropped.
05
Reasons go to the model
Write the deny reason as an instruction, not as an error message; it becomes the next prompt.

Tiles

Four scenarios, each with its own color band and icon.

01
Cloud-first team
All guardrails in .github/hooks on main, bash only, evidence through an http hook to the SIEM. The same file protects the CLI on laptops.
02
Regulated desktop
Policy hooks in policy.d, root-owned, plus allowManagedHooksOnly in the MDM settings. Developers keep their own hooks for convenience, never as policy.
03
Multi-tool shop
One .claude/settings.json with PascalCase events serves Claude Code, VS Code and the GitHub Copilot CLI. Scripts branch on tool_name.
04
Internal product
SDK callbacks apply product rules and ship telemetry to the app tracer; file hooks from the platform team still apply underneath.

Story tiles

The same four, told as incidents that never happened.

01
Force push to main
preToolUse deny on git push --force to protected branches; the reason sends the agent to open a PR. Rulesets already blocked it server-side; the hook saves the round trip.
02
Secrets in the shell
Deny curl piped to bash and any command with a token flag; log the redacted attempt. The SIEM sees a pattern before a person does.
03
The payments folder
ask on edits under src/payments and deny in the cloud; the reviewer sees every touch with a diff, never a surprise.
04
Untrusted web content
postToolUse on web_fetch strips instruction-like lines and marks the result as untrusted. Cheap, and it fires on every fetch, subagents included.

Cards and the why block

Three ideas, then why it matters, the impact and the trap.

Format

Prettier after edits

PostToolUse runs prettier --write on edited files. The agent never argues about style again and the diff stays clean.

Lint and links

Fix what the tool just broke

Run the linter on the touched file and hand the findings back as additionalContext, capped at 10 KB.

Annotate

Tell the model what it cannot see

Coverage numbers, the owner of the file, the ticket the change belongs to, joined from all hooks with a blank line.

Why it mattersthe model only sees what the payload carries
The impactreview comments about style drop to zero in a week
The trapa ten-second linter on every edit turns a two-minute task into twenty

def dijkstra(graph, src):
    dist = {v: inf for v in graph}
    dist[src] = 0
    heap = [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heappop(heap)
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if d + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = d + w
                heappush(heap, (dist[v], v))
Compare

Two worlds side by side, with a vs badge in the middle.

Permissions and the sandbox

Permission rules say which tools and arguments the agent may use; the sandbox limits what a call can reach. Both are declarative and blind to context: they cannot read the payload, log it, transform it or decide by time of day.

Hooks

Code you own, run by the runtime at fourteen moments with the full payload: the command about to run, the prompt just typed, the result just produced. It can deny, modify, inject context, notify or ship evidence.

Same file, three toolsGitHub Copilot CLI, VS Code and Claude Code read the same hooks file.
Declarative firstStart with permission rules; add a hook when a decision needs the payload.
Never both for one ruleOne control per concern, or two teams will argue about which one fired.

Do and don't

Symptom on the left in red, correction on the right in green.

Don't
  • "blocked by policy" as the deny reason
  • a guardrail that calls a remote service on preToolUse
  • the same rule in permissions, a hook and the sandbox
  • starting the program with policy hooks
  • logging the raw command with tokens in it
Do
  • "Destructive delete. Use a scoped path." as the reason
  • a local script under one second, network on postToolUse only
  • one control per concern, the non-negotiable one in managed settings
  • a banner and a log first, policy in month three
  • sed the six token patterns before any write

Questions and answers

The five questions every workshop asks in the first hour.

Does a hook replace permission rules?
No. Rules are declarative and cheap; a hook reads the payload. Use rules for tool kinds and a hook for decisions that need context.
What happens on a timeout?
The tool runs. Every timeout fails open, even for policy hooks; only a crash on preToolUse denies.
Can the developer turn it off?
User, repository and inline hooks honor disableAllHooks. Policy hooks and managed settings do not.
Where does the deny reason go?
Back to the model as the next instruction, so it changes the next attempt instead of triggering a retry.
Does the cloud agent run my hooks?
Only .github/hooks on the default branch, bash entries only; no user files, no policy hooks, no plugins.

Glossary

Sixteen terms, numbered, in four colors.

Hook
A command, HTTP call or prompt the runtime executes at a lifecycle event, JSON in and JSON out.
Event
One of fourteen moments in a session, from sessionStart to sessionEnd.
preToolUse
The only event that can deny a tool call, with allow, deny or ask.
agentStop
Fires when the agent wants to end the turn; block forces another one.
Matcher
A regex anchored as ^(?:PATTERN)$ against the tool or agent name.
PascalCase alias
Stop, PreToolUse: names compatible with Claude and VS Code.
Fail-closed
A crashed preToolUse hook denies; a timeout never does.
Policy hook
Admin-installed in policy.d; loads first, cannot be disabled.
disableAllHooks
The documented switch for user, repo and inline hooks.
additionalContext
Text injected into the session, capped at 10 KB.
stop_hook_active
True on the forced turn after a block.
http hook
A POST to an https endpoint with allowedEnvVars headers.
Permission rule
Declarative allow, deny or ask by tool kind and argument pattern.
Sandbox bypass
A tool call that is never pre-approved.
Managed settings
JSON managed by MDM or server; most restrictive wins.
Safe output
The Agentic Workflows equivalent of a guardrail.

function binarySearch(a, x) {

}

def dijkstra(graph, src):

function binarySearch(a, x) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
  while (lo <= hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (a[mid] === x) return mid;
    a[mid] < x ? lo = mid + 1 : hi = mid - 1;
  }
  return -1;
}

Type in, print out

A payload goes in on stdin. A decision comes out on stdout.

stdin is the whole storyEvent, session id, tool name and the raw toolArgs string arrive as one JSON object. Parse it twice: the object, then the command inside.
stdout is the decisionOne JSON object, nothing else. permissionDecision plus a reason the agent can act on; progress lines are stripped, two objects are ignored.
Exit codes carry meaningExit 0 parses stdout; exit 2 is a deny on the gates; other errors fail open, except preToolUse. Timeouts always fail open.

Converge into one

Six files, one merged configuration, always in this order.

Policy loads firstpolicy.d and the registry are root-owned, load before trust is evaluated and ignore disableAllHooks. That is the admin lane.
Repo and user merge.github/hooks, ~/.copilot/hooks and the two settings.json all contribute; the repository overrides the user per key, nothing is replaced wholesale.
Plugins close the listPlugin hooks load last and can be forced or blocked by managed settings. The cloud agent reads only the repository file.

fn merge(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> {
    let (mut i, mut j) = (0, 0);
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(a.len() + b.len());
    while i < a.len() && j < b.len() {
        if a[i] <= b[j] { out.push(a[i]); i += 1 }
        else { out.push(b[j]); j += 1 }
    }
    out
}
Pass or bounce

Two commands reach preToolUse. One passes. One comes back with a reason.

allow is silentnpm test matches nothing in the deny list; the hook exits 0 with allow and the runtime moves on to the permission service.
deny bounces with a reasonThe destructive delete never runs. The reason goes back to the model as the next instruction, so it proposes a scoped path instead of retrying.
preToolUse is fail-closedA crashed hook here denies the tool; a timeout does not. Keep the script local, under a second, and free of network calls.

Loop with a traveling dot

The agent wants to stop. The hook says: not before the tests.

block forces one more turnagentStop returns decision block with a reason; the runtime starts a new turn with that reason as the prompt. Eight blocks maximum.
stop_hook_active is the memoryOn the forced turn the flag is true. Check it first, or your hook blocks the same stop forever and the CLI ends the turn anyway.
Proof, then stopThe hook reads the test log, not the model. When the log says pass, decision allow, and the session ends with evidence.

Packets on lanes

What leaves the laptop, by which door, and what never does.

The http hook is the SIEM doorA POST per event with the session id, the decision and the redacted command. Only https, headers from allowedEnvVars, five second timeout.
Spans prove the guardrail ranhook.start, hook.end and hook.error ride the session trace with traceparent; one query answers whether the deny fired and how long it took.
The audit log is not enoughGitHub records agent sessions and actors, never local prompts or arguments. If the evidence has to include the command, a hook has to ship it.

Flip and lock

Three switches the developer can flip. One they cannot.

disableAllHooks reaches threeUser, repository and inline hooks can all be switched off from a file the developer owns. Useful for debugging, useless as a control.
Policy hooks stay lockedRoot-owned files in policy.d or the registry load first, in every session, regardless of trust, and no flag turns them off.
Managed settings close the gapsallowManagedHooksOnly, deny rules and disableBypassPermissionsMode arrive through the MDM and beat every local value.

Rise step by step

Four steps, ninety days, from a session banner to a policy nobody turns off.

Start by watchingA banner and a JSONL log cost an afternoon and teach the payload. Nobody argues with a hook that only observes.
Then protect and automateDeny the five destructive patterns with reasons, gate the stop on tests, format after edits, ship events to the SIEM. Measure false denies per week.
Govern last, on purposePolicy hooks, managed settings and a platform plugin come after trust exists. A program that starts here is disabled by lunchtime.

The agent pushes whatever it believes is done. Tests are a claim in the summary.
02
No evidence
The audit log shows a session existed. Nothing about what ran.
03
Everyone can disable
disableAllHooks in a file the developer owns.
01
agentStop gate
Block until the test log says pass; one forced turn, then a clean stop.
02
Evidence shipped
http hook to the SIEM plus OTLP spans with the session id.
03
Policy the developer cannot edit
policy.d via MDM and managed permissions.

function binarySearch(a, x) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
  while (lo <= hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (a[mid] === x) return mid;
    a[mid] < x ? lo = mid + 1 : hi = mid - 1;
  }
  return -1;
}
